evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration describes a 33-mile drive taking one to two hours, with views of the wild river and a finish at historic Rogue River Ranch.
evidence.quote: Length 33 mi / 53.1 km Time to Allow 1-2 hours

evidence.quote: This overlook offers spectacular views of the mighty waterfalls, surrounding forests, and the Wild and Scenic Rogue River.

evidence.claim: The road’s destination grew from a one-room cabin in the late nineteenth century into the ranch complex at the end of the route.
evidence.quote: Dating back to the late 1800s, the ranch grew from a one-room cabin to what it is today.

evidence.claim: Travel through this canyon has taken several forms: the riverside trail was developed by the Takelma Indians and later improved by miners and settlers.
evidence.quote: This historic trail was originally developed by the Takelma Indians and improved by miners and settlers as they moved deeper into the canyon.

evidence.claim: A suspension bridge built in 1908 was washed away in the flood of 1927, leaving an abutment visible from Rainie Falls Overlook.
evidence.quote: This 13-foot tall abutment is one of the few remnants of a suspension bridge constructed in 1908 but washed out by the flood of 1927.

evidence.claim: From the Merlin exit, follow Merlin-Galice Road for 23 miles, cross Graves Creek Bridge and turn onto Mt. Reuben Road.
evidence.quote: Take I-5 north to exit 61, Merlin exit. Turn left and continue northwest on the Merlin-Galice Road for 23 miles. Continue across the Graves Creek Bridge. Turn left onto the Mt. Reuben Road

evidence.claim: Rainie Falls Overlook is 1.3 miles along that road.
evidence.quote: Turn left onto the Mt. Reuben Road (BLM 34-8-1) for 1.3 miles. Rainie Falls Overlook is on the left-hand side of the road.

evidence.claim: The mountain drive continues to Rogue River Ranch at the byway’s end, where the preserved buildings mark the former center of Marial.

evidence.quote: Parallel to the wild stretch of the river, the Lower Rogue River Trail winds through the Wild Rogue Wilderness between the mouth of Grave Creek and Illahe.

evidence.claim: Rogue River Ranch’s main house faces Mule Creek, its lumber hand-cut from ponderosa pine logs felled on the site.
evidence.quote: It sits on a gentle slope facing Mule Creek. The house is a two-story, wood-frame structure. The lumber for the house was all cut by hand from Ponderosa pine logs cut on the site.

evidence.claim: George Billings built the house in 1903 and established a trading company at Marial.
evidence.quote: In 1903, George Billings constructed a large two-story house and established the Billings Trading Company at Marial.

evidence.claim: The settlement followed the Rogue River Wars and the forced removal of most Takelma and other Native people along the river.
evidence.quote: After the Rogue River Wars of 1855–56 and the forced removal of most of the Takelma and other native people who lived along the river, a small number of newcomers began to settle along or near the canyon.

evidence.claim: The ranch passed to Stanley Anderson in 1931 and to the federal government in 1970.
evidence.quote: In 1931, Billings sold his 70-acre (280,000 m2) ranch to Stanley Anderson for $5,000.

evidence.claim: and to the federal government in 1970.
evidence.quote: In 1970, the Anderson family sold their 200-acre (0.81 km2) ranch to the United States Government

evidence.claim: The Bureau of Land Management converted the main house into a museum covering Native American history, mining and the ranch families.
evidence.quote: The Bureau of Land Management established the Rogue River Ranch National Historic Site and converted the main house into a museum. The museum has displays on Native American history, the local mining era, the Billings homestead period, and the development of the Anderson family farm.

evidence.claim: For travel beyond Galice-Hellgate toward the ranch, BLM advises a full fuel tank, first aid kit, food and water. Roads beyond that byway are often closed by winter snow.
evidence.quote: If you plan on continuing your travel beyond this byway route be sure to have a full tank of gas, a first aid kit, food, and water with you as you will be traveling into remote country with no services. Roads beyond this byway route are often closed in winter, due to snow accumulation.
